concepts.title: Redundancy and Failover
concepts.description: Every component in a system will eventually fail. The design question is whether something else is already in place to take over, and how quickly and cleanly the handoff happens.
learningObjectives: Define a single point of failure and explain why eliminating one always requires an independently-failing redundant component, not just a more reliable version of the same one.
Distinguish active-active from active-passive redundancy and explain the cost/complexity tradeoff between them.
Explain what failover actually requires beyond having a spare: detection, redirection, and state recovery.
Explain why redundant components must fail independently, and identify common hidden shared-fate risks (same rack, same AZ, same deploy, same config).
Evaluate a proposed redundancy design and identify whether it has actually removed a single point of failure or only relocated it.

sections.heading: Single Points of Failure
sections.body: A **single point of failure (SPOF)** is any one component whose failure, alone, is enough to take down the whole system: one database, one load balancer, one network link, one region. Plan on it failing eventually: disks die, processes crash, kernels panic, cloud hosts get retired for maintenance, engineers fat-finger a config push. **Redundancy** is the practice of having more than one of a critical component so that no single failure is fatal to the system as a whole. Redundancy only removes a SPOF if the copies fail *independently*. The arithmetic shows how much depends on that word. Two servers that are each up 99% of the time, failing independently, are both down only 0.01% of the time (0.01 x 0.01), so the pair is up 99.99%. If both sit behind one switch that is up 99.9%, the pair can't do better than about 99.9%. Two things that fail together are still one point of failure.

sections.heading: Active-Active vs. Active-Passive
sections.body:
**Active-passive** redundancy keeps a standby instance ready but idle while the primary serves everything; on failure, the standby is promoted. Only one thing serves traffic at a time, so there are no two live copies to reconcile. In exchange, the standby's capacity is wasted while things are healthy, and failover takes time (detecting the failure, promoting the standby, redirecting traffic) during which the system is down. Idle standbys also rot: one that hasn't been failed over to in a year may have an expired certificate or a missing permission, so practise the failover.

**Active-active** redundancy keeps multiple instances simultaneously serving live traffic, typically behind a load balancer. When one is lost, the others absorb its share of the load, often with no visible downtime if they have spare capacity. The cost is complexity when the instances hold state: several active copies of a database, cache, or queue have to be kept consistent or reconciled, which brings back the replication and consistency tradeoffs from earlier modules. As a rule of thumb, use active-active where the workload allows it (stateless services are the easy case) and active-passive where several simultaneous writers would be the harder problem. A primary database commonly runs active-passive with synchronous or near-synchronous standbys to avoid the write conflicts of multi-leader replication.

sections.heading: Failover: Detection, Redirection, Recovery
sections.body:
A spare is necessary but not sufficient; most of the reliability work is in the failover *process*, which has three parts. **Detection**: something has to notice the primary is unhealthy. This is the health checking from the load-balancing lesson, with the same failure modes: a check that passes while the request path is broken, and the delay of waiting for enough consecutive failures to rule out a blip. **Redirection**: traffic (or write ownership, for a database) has to move to the surviving component: a load balancer pulling an unhealthy backend from rotation, a DNS or virtual-IP change pointing at a new primary, or a consensus-based leader election promoting a new leader. **Recovery of state**: the component taking over has to be able to serve correctly. A promoted database replica needs to be caught up (or you accept the unreplicated writes as lost), and a new service instance needs whatever session or in-flight state the failed one held. A stateless service has nothing to recover, so it fails over as soon as the failure is detected.

Databases add a danger of their own. If the old primary was only cut off from the monitor, promoting the standby leaves two primaries accepting writes (split brain). Failover tools prevent this with *fencing*: before the new primary takes writes, the old one is powered off, loses its storage, or loses a lease it needs in order to accept writes.

sections.heading: Shared Fate
sections.body: A common redundancy mistake is building two things that *look* independent but share a dependency that can take both down at once. Two database replicas in the same physical rack both go dark when that rack loses power. Two application servers that are containers on the same host both die when that host's kernel panics. Two 'independent' services that both depend on the same third-party API, or the same shared config file, or were both deployed via the same faulty script, fail together the moment that shared thing breaks. None of these show up on the component diagram. They show up when you ask 'what has to go wrong for *both* of these to fail at the same time?' and keep asking it down through the infrastructure: same availability zone, same region, same cloud provider, same deploy pipeline, same person able to delete both with one mistaken command. Deploys and config pushes deserve the most suspicion, because they reach every copy at once by design. Rolling a change out to one instance or one zone first is a redundancy measure too.

sections.heading: How Much Redundancy Is Enough
sections.body: Every standby or active-active peer costs money and is one more thing to patch, monitor, and reason about, so stop adding redundancy once you meet your availability target. Derive the amount from that target and from a list of correlated failure modes. A 99.9% target allows about 43 minutes of downtime in a 30-day month; 99.99% allows about 4.3 minutes, less than it takes most people to wake up and log in, so every failover has to be automatic. N+1 redundancy (one spare beyond what's needed for normal load) tolerates any single failure; multi-region redundancy protects against a failure mode single-region N+1 cannot (the entire region going down), at a much higher cost and complexity, including the cross-region consistency questions from the CAP lesson. Write down which failures the system must survive (one host, one zone, one region, one bad deploy) and buy redundancy for those.

examples.title: Redundancy That Isn't: Two 'Independent' Replicas, One Rack
examples.code:
DESIGN AS DRAWN:
  [Primary DB] ---- replicates to ----> [Replica DB]
  "We have a replica, so we're protected against a database failure."

DESIGN AS ACTUALLY DEPLOYED:
  Rack 14: [Primary DB]  [Replica DB]   <- same rack, same power feed,
                                            same network switch

Incident: Rack 14's power distribution unit fails.
Both Primary DB and Replica DB go offline AT THE SAME TIME.
"We had a replica" did not help at all -- the physical
single point of failure was the rack's shared power, not the database
software, and nobody had traced the dependency that far down.
examples.explanation: The diagram shows two databases, and there is a replica, but nobody asked what single thing could take both down below the database layer. No database setting fixes this; placement does. Put the replica in a different rack, ideally in a different availability zone, so that losing power, networking, or cooling in one location doesn't affect the other. Cloud providers expose availability zones for this purpose: resources in different zones don't share power, cooling, or a building. Managed services still make you choose. A single-AZ RDS instance with a read replica in the same AZ has the rack-14 problem with better marketing. And a replica in another zone protects against hardware failure only: a bad `DELETE` reaches it in milliseconds.

examples.title: Active-Passive Failover Timeline for a Database
examples.code:
t=0.0s   Primary DB stops responding (crashed)
t=0.0s-6.0s   Health checks failing, but requiring 3 consecutive failures
              at 2s intervals before declaring it unhealthy (avoids flapping
              on a single blip) -- system is DOWN for writes this whole time
t=6.0s   Primary declared unhealthy; failover process begins
t=6.0s-9.0s   Standby replica promoted to primary; DNS/virtual IP updated
              to point at the new primary
t=9.0s-11.0s  Application connection pools reconnect (some still holding
              stale connections to the dead primary until their own
              retry/reconnect logic kicks in)
t=11.0s  System fully recovered -- ~11 seconds of write downtime total
examples.explanation: With a standby ready, about 11 seconds still passed between the crash and full recovery: 6 to be confident it wasn't a blip, 3 to promote and redirect, 2 for clients to reconnect. That is a good outcome, and managed databases often quote 30 to 120 seconds for the same thing. 'We have a standby' means a bounded recovery time, and you tune the bound. Checking every second would detect the crash in 3 seconds, at the price of failing over on a 3-second network hiccup, which is an outage you caused. The last phase is often the longest in practice, because clients that cache DNS beyond its TTL or keep pooled connections to a dead address can hang for minutes unless you set connect and socket timeouts.

examples.title: Active-Active: Losing One of Four With No User-Visible Downtime
examples.code:
4 stateless app servers, active-active, behind a load balancer,
each normally running at ~60% CPU (headroom reserved on purpose)

Server 2 crashes:
  [LB] -> server1 (60% -> 80% CPU, absorbing extra share)
       -> server2 (CRASHED, removed from rotation by health check)
       -> server3 (60% -> 80% CPU)
       -> server4 (60% -> 80% CPU)

No request is ever routed TO server2 after the health check catches it
(typically within a few seconds). The other three absorb the load
immediately because they were ALREADY serving live traffic --
there is no promotion step, no DNS change, nothing to "become active."
examples.explanation: The survivors were already serving traffic, so nothing has to be promoted; the only delay is the health check noticing and excluding server2. Requests sent to it before that still fail, unless the load balancer retries them on another server, which is safe only for idempotent requests. This works because the servers are stateless: any of the other three can serve a request that would have gone to server2. The price is the headroom. Total load is 4 x 60% = 240% of one server, so three servers carry 80% each and two would need 120%: this pool survives one failure, not two. Autoscaling on CPU needs the same arithmetic, because a target of 80% across four servers leaves 107% for three.

misconceptions.description: Having a backup or replica of a component automatically means that component is no longer a single point of failure.
misconceptions.clarification: A backup only removes a SPOF if it can fail independently of the primary. A replica in the same rack, same availability zone, sharing the same power or network path, or deployed via the same script as the primary, is still exposed to whatever failure would take out the shared dependency, and then both go down together. To get redundancy you can count on, trace the shared dependencies (power, network, physical location, deploy pipeline, config) and place the second copy outside them. Then test it by turning the primary off.
misconceptions.fact: A backup only removes a SPOF if it can fail independently of the primary.

misconceptions.description: Active-active is strictly better than active-passive, so it should always be preferred when redundancy is being designed.
misconceptions.clarification: Active-active avoids the failover delay and wasted idle capacity of active-passive, but it requires multiple instances to be simultaneously live and, if they share state, kept consistent with each other while all serving traffic. That reintroduces the write-conflict and coordination problems from the replication and CAP lessons. For components where keeping multiple simultaneous writers consistent is the hard problem (a primary database is the classic case), active-passive with a single writer is often the lower-risk design. It accepts a bounded failover delay and never has to resolve two conflicting writes.

exercises.prompt: A team runs two application servers, both stateless, behind a load balancer configured with active-active routing and health checks (3 consecutive failures at 2-second intervals to mark unhealthy). Server A crashes hard (process dies instantly) at t=10.0s. Predict what happens to in-flight and new requests between t=10.0s and t=16.0s, and explain why statelessness matters to your answer.
exercises.code:
2 servers, active-active, behind LB
Health check: every 2s, 3 consecutive failures required to mark unhealthy
Server A crashes (process dies) at t=10.0s
Server B is healthy throughout
hints: Work out when the LB will have accumulated 3 consecutive failed health checks against server A, given checks happen every 2 seconds starting from some point at or after t=10.0s.
Until server A is marked unhealthy, does the LB still route SOME new requests to it? What happens to those specific requests?
Server B is healthy and stateless the entire time -- does it need any data or context from server A to correctly serve requests that would have gone to A?
exercises.expectedAnswer: Requests in flight on A at t=10.0s fail, because the process handling them is gone. New requests routed to A until it is marked unhealthy also fail, usually fast with "connection refused" since only the process died. The first failed check comes at most 2s after the crash and two more follow at 2s intervals, so A is excluded somewhere between t=14.0s and t=16.0s; until then roughly half of new requests fail (unless the LB retries them on B). Requests routed to server B throughout are unaffected and succeed normally, since B never went down. By t=16.0s at the latest the LB has seen 3 consecutive failures and removes A, and from then on all new requests go to B, which must have the capacity for twice its usual load. Statelessness matters because server B doesn't need to recover or reconstruct any data that was 'only on server A'. Once A is excluded, service is restored with no separate recovery step.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Health-check detection sets the length of the failure window. If a check happened to run just after the crash, the failures land at about t=10, 12, and 14; if one ran just before, they land at about t=12, 14, and 16. So the window is 4 to 6 seconds, plus the check timeout if the host hangs instead of refusing connections. During it, the share of requests the LB sends to A (about half here) fails while B's succeed. A shorter interval or a lower threshold narrows the window but risks excluding a healthy server on a blip. Many load balancers also watch live traffic (passive checks) and stop using a backend after a few refused connections, which closes the window sooner. After exclusion there is nothing to promote or recover, because both servers are stateless and B could already serve any request. B now runs at double its earlier load, so a pair of servers each at 60% would pass the failover and then fall over.

exercises.prompt: A team believes they've eliminated their single point of failure by running two identical Kubernetes pods for their payments service. During a cloud provider incident affecting one physical host, BOTH pods go down simultaneously, even though they were supposed to be independent. Diagnose what likely went wrong and describe the fix.
exercises.code:
Deployment config (simplified):
  replicas: 2
  # no anti-affinity or topology spread rule specified -- the scheduler
  # has only a soft default preference for spreading pods, and can
  # place both on the SAME node when it finds capacity there

Actual placement chosen by the scheduler that day:
  Node 47: payments-pod-1, payments-pod-2   <- both landed on the SAME node

Incident: Node 47 experiences a hardware fault and is taken offline.
Both payments-pod-1 and payments-pod-2 go down together.
hints: Two pods existing is not the same guarantee as two pods running on independently failing hardware. What determines which node each pod lands on?
Without an explicit rule telling it otherwise, does a Kubernetes scheduler guarantee that two replicas land on different nodes, or does it only prefer it when other factors allow?
Look for a scheduling constraint that forces replicas apart, at the node level and ideally the availability-zone level too.
exercises.solutionCode:
Deployment config (fixed):
  replicas: 2
  affinity:                    # goes in the pod template's spec
    podAntiAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        - labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: payments-service
          topologyKey: "kubernetes.io/hostname"   # forces different NODES
          # for stronger guarantees, also add a rule with
          # topologyKey: "topology.kubernetes.io/zone" to force different AZs
exercises.solutionExplanation: The deployment asked for 2 replicas but never required them to be on separate infrastructure. Kubernetes' default topology spreading is a scoring preference: if the other nodes were full, cordoned, or scored lower for other reasons that day, both pods can land on Node 47, and nothing moves them apart later. That node's hardware became a single point of failure for a service that looked redundant on paper. The required anti-affinity rule keyed on hostname makes the scheduler refuse to co-locate them, and the pod stays Pending if it can't comply. Think about that before applying it: on a two-node cluster, a rolling update that surges a third pod would be stuck, and during a node drain the replacement has nowhere to go. `topologySpreadConstraints` with `maxSkew: 1` is often the better tool with more replicas, since it evens pods out across nodes and zones without limiting you to one per node. Two pods on two nodes can still share a zone, so add the zone key if a zone outage must not stop payments. Add a PodDisruptionBudget too, so that a drain doesn't evict both at once.

assessments.prompt: A team's disaster-recovery plan for their primary database is a nightly snapshot stored in the same region and availability zone as the primary database itself. What is the main reliability gap in this plan?
options: The snapshot and the primary database can both be lost together in a single availability-zone-level failure, and the snapshot's age also means up to nearly 24 hours of writes could be lost even if it survives, so there is no independently failing backup.
Nightly snapshots take too much CPU to be practical.
Databases cannot be restored from snapshots without significant downtime under any circumstances.
Snapshots are only useful for read scaling, not for disaster recovery.
assessments.explanation: The plan has two gaps: a shared-fate risk (the snapshot lives in the same AZ as the primary, so whatever takes out the AZ takes out both) and a recovery-point gap (a nightly cadence means, in the worst case, almost a full day of writes are unrecoverable even when the snapshot itself is fine). The “Nightly snapshots take too much CPU to be practical” option is at most a minor operational cost. The “Snapshots are only useful for read scaling…” option is wrong: snapshots are a standard disaster-recovery tool, but this one is kept in the wrong place and taken too rarely. The “Databases cannot be restored from snapshots without…” option overstates a separate concern (recovery time): restores do take time, but some can be brought up alongside the running system.

assessments.prompt: A stakeholder says: "We're fully protected against downtime -- we have two of everything." Explain what's incomplete about this statement and walk through the questions you'd ask to verify it.
assessments.modelAnswer: Having two of a component is necessary but not sufficient. Redundancy is supposed to mean that a single failure can't take the system down, and that only holds if the two components fail independently. 'We have two of everything' says that multiple instances exist, and says nothing about whether they can fail together. I'd trace the dependency graph one or two layers past the component diagram and ask: are the two instances in the same physical rack, the same availability zone, or the same region? If so, what happens to both when that shared location has a power, network, or cooling failure? Were they deployed via the same script or pipeline, and could a single bad deploy or a misconfigured rollout push a bad change to both simultaneously instead of one at a time? Do they share a config file, a secrets store, or a feature flag system, such that a single mistake there (a bad credential rotation, an accidental deletion) affects both at once? Do they depend on the same third-party service or the same upstream dependency, such that its outage takes out both redundant paths equally? Beyond shared fate, I'd also ask about the failover mechanism itself, since owning a spare doesn't automatically mean a fast or correct handoff: how is a failure detected, how long does that take, what redirects traffic or promotes a replacement, does the replacement need to recover any state first, and can the survivor carry the full load? Finally: when was it last tested? An untested failover is a guess, so I'd schedule a drill that turns one of the two off. Redundancy is real protection only when each of these questions has a verified answer; "two of everything" is where that conversation starts.

assessments.prompt: A primary database uses active-passive redundancy with a single synchronous standby, while a fleet of stateless web servers uses active-active redundancy. Why does the database favor active-passive when active-active usually recovers faster?
options: Because active-passive redundancy is cheaper in every case, regardless of what the component does.
Because active-active redundancy is only supported for components running on Kubernetes, and most databases do not run on Kubernetes.
Because databases are always slower than web servers, so active-passive is required to keep latency low.

Because keeping multiple simultaneous writers to the same data consistent with each other reintroduces the write-conflict and consistency-coordination problems from multi-leader replication, making a single clear writer (active-passive) the more tractable design for this component.
assessments.explanation: Two active database writers can accept conflicting changes to the same row, and someone has to reconcile them; a single writer orders everything. Stateless web servers are the easy case for active-active because they hold no writable state to reconcile. The “Because databases are always slower than web…” option is about latency, which active-passive doesn't improve (a synchronous standby adds some). The “Because active-active redundancy is only supported…” option is fabricated: active-active long predates Kubernetes. The “Because active-passive redundancy is cheaper in every…” option makes cost the deciding factor, and it isn't even always true: an idle standby is capacity you pay for and don't use.

assessments.prompt: Why does a stateless service fail over almost instantly compared to a stateful one like a database?
options: Because stateless services always use active-passive redundancy, which fails over faster than active-active.
Because stateless services do not require health checks to detect a failure.
Because a stateless service has no state-recovery step to wait on.
Because stateless services are always hosted on faster hardware than stateful ones.
assessments.explanation: With no session, cache, or data held locally, failover is finished as soon as the failure is detected and traffic moves. A promoted database replica has to be caught up (or its missing writes written off) and the old primary fenced before it can serve correctly. The “Because stateless services are always hosted…” option invents an unrelated hardware-speed claim. The “Because stateless services do not require health…” option is false: detection is still required, and only the state-recovery step is skipped. The “Because stateless services always use active-passive redundancy…” option is backwards: stateless services usually run active-active.

assessments.prompt: What is the key diagnostic question to ask when evaluating whether two redundant components are independent?
options: "Do the two components run the exact same version of the software?"
"What has to go wrong for BOTH of these to fail at the same time?".
"How many total requests per second can each component handle individually?"
"Which of the two components is more expensive to operate?"
assessments.explanation: Asking what would take BOTH down, and tracing the answer through zone, host, network, pipeline, and config, is what exposes shared fate; the component diagram alone hides it. The “"Do the two components run the exact…” option asks about version parity. A bug in a shared version is one possible common cause, but the question covers only that one. The “"Which of the two components is more…” and “"How many total requests per second can…” options ask about cost and raw capacity respectively, neither of which addresses whether the components can fail together.

concepts.title: Circuit Breakers: Preventing Cascading Failure
concepts.description: When a downstream dependency turns unhealthy, the worst thing an upstream service can do is keep calling it at full speed and waiting on every failed attempt. A circuit breaker breaks that loop by failing fast on purpose.
learningObjectives: Explain how a synchronously-called unhealthy dependency can consume caller resources and cause a cascading failure across unrelated code paths.
Describe the three circuit breaker states (closed, open, half-open) and the transition rule between each.
Explain why 'failing fast' via an open circuit is a deliberate reliability improvement, not merely giving up.
Distinguish a circuit breaker from a simple timeout and from a retry policy, and explain how the three are meant to work together.
Design a reasonable fallback behavior for a circuit in the open state, appropriate to a given feature's importance.

sections.heading: How a Downstream Failure Becomes an Upstream Outage
sections.body: When service A calls service B synchronously and B becomes slow or unresponsive (degraded, hanging, or timing out, which is harder to detect and route around than a clean crash), A's calls to B don't fail instantly. They sit and wait, typically until A's own timeout fires. Each waiting call holds a thread, a connection, or some other finite resource in A. How many pile up is simple to estimate (Little's law): calls in flight = arrival rate x time per call. At 100 calls per second and 80 ms each, 8 are in flight. If B starts taking 8 seconds, the same traffic needs 800. If A has a pool of 200 threads, it is exhausted in about 2 seconds, and A becomes unresponsive to *its* callers with no bug in its own code. This is a **cascading failure**: an unhealthy dependency several layers down takes out healthy services above it by exhausting resources at each hop.

sections.heading: The Three States: Closed, Open, Half-Open
sections.body: A **circuit breaker** wraps a call to a dependency and tracks its recent success/failure rate, moving through three states named after an electrical circuit breaker's. **Closed** is the normal state: calls pass through to the dependency as usual, and the breaker counts failures. If failures cross a configured threshold (say, more than 50% of calls failing over the last 10 seconds, or 5 consecutive failures), the breaker trips to **open**: for a configured cooldown period, calls are rejected immediately, without attempting the network call, typically by raising an error or invoking a fallback. While open, the caller sends no load to a dependency that's already struggling, and spends none of its own resources waiting on calls that would probably fail. After the cooldown elapses, the breaker moves to **half-open**: it allows a small number of trial calls through to test whether the dependency has recovered. If those succeed, the breaker closes again and normal traffic resumes; if they fail, it reopens and the cooldown starts over.

sections.heading: Why Failing Fast Helps
sections.body: It can feel backwards that refusing to try counts as a reliability improvement. But once a dependency is unhealthy, the call was very likely going to fail anyway, and what you control is *how* it fails. Waiting for a timeout is expensive: it holds a thread or connection for the full timeout, on every call, when the system can least afford it. Failing at the breaker takes microseconds and frees the caller to serve other requests or invoke a fallback. It also takes load off the dependency. A service that is overloaded and restarting often can't come back because callers keep hitting it with full traffic plus retries; a few seconds of quiet may be what lets it warm its caches and recover. Some calls that would have succeeded get rejected while the breaker is open. That is the price, and it is why the threshold is usually a failure rate over a minimum number of calls: 1 failure out of 2 calls at 3 a.m. should not open it.

sections.heading: Circuit Breakers, Timeouts, and Retries Together
sections.body: These three solve different problems. A **timeout** bounds how long any single call may wait; without one, a hanging dependency can block a caller indefinitely. A **retry policy** decides whether, and how, to try again after a call fails, with backoff and jitter (a randomized delay, so clients don't all retry at the same instant) to avoid a retry storm. Retry only idempotent operations, and only at one layer: three layers that each make 3 attempts turn one user request into 27 calls at the bottom. A **circuit breaker** works one level up: it watches the *aggregate* pattern of successes and failures across many calls and stops attempting calls for a while, whatever the individual call's timeout or retry settings. A good call path uses all three: a timeout on each attempt, a small number of retries with backoff for likely-transient failures, and a breaker that stops both once the dependency is down. Without the breaker, retries from many callers keep load flowing toward an overwhelmed dependency for as long as the outage lasts. The breaker in turn depends on the timeout, because a call that hangs forever is never counted as a failure. State is usually kept per process, so each of 40 instances trips its own breaker.

sections.heading: Choosing a Fallback for the Open State
sections.body: A circuit breaker makes you decide something that's easy to skip while everything works: what should the caller do when the call isn't attempted? It depends on how critical the dependency is to the feature. For recommendations on a product page, omit the section or show a generic, cached, or default set; a degraded page beats a failed one. For payment authorization, no safe fallback can make up an answer, so fail the operation clearly and quickly: the user gets a fast 'try again shortly' instead of a slow hang or an order nobody paid for. In between are fallbacks with limits, such as a cached shipping rate that is fine for an hour but not for a week, or accepting an order into a queue to be charged later. If the open circuit only surfaces as an unhandled exception, the feature fails just as badly as before, only faster. Alert when a breaker opens, because a good fallback hides the outage from everyone, including you.

examples.title: A Recommendations Service Timeout Cascading Into the Whole Product Page
examples.code:
Product page service calls 3 dependencies to render a page:
  1. inventory_service   (fast, healthy)
  2. pricing_service      (fast, healthy)
  3. recommendations_service  (degraded -- taking 8s per call instead of 80ms)

WITHOUT a circuit breaker on the recommendations call:
  Every page render waits up to 8s on step 3 (or its own timeout) before
  continuing -- product page latency balloons from ~200ms to 8+ seconds.
  Under real traffic, the product page service's own thread pool fills up
  with requests stuck waiting on recommendations_service, and even
  requests that don't care about recommendations start failing.

WITH a circuit breaker on the recommendations call:
  Each call has a 500ms timeout, so a slow call counts as a FAILURE.
  After the failure threshold trips (e.g. 50% failures over 10s), the
  breaker opens. Subsequent calls fail IMMEDIATELY (no 8s wait), the
  page renders WITHOUT the recommendations section (fallback: omit it),
  and total page latency stays close to ~200ms even while
  recommendations_service remains unhealthy.
examples.explanation: recommendations_service is equally broken in both scenarios. Without the breaker, every page render waits on it, and the threads stuck waiting risk taking down the ENTIRE page, including the inventory and pricing data that were never in trouble. With the breaker, the failure stays in the section that depends on the unhealthy service. Note the timeout: an 8-second response is a successful call as far as a plain breaker can tell, so without the 500 ms limit it would never trip. (Some libraries, such as Resilience4j, can also count slow calls as failures.) During the first seconds, before the threshold is reached, pages take up to 500 ms longer, and after that they are back near 200 ms.

examples.title: Circuit Breaker State Machine in Code
examples.explanation: While `closed`, the breaker lets calls through and counts consecutive failures, tripping to `open` at the threshold. While `open`, it skips the dependency and goes straight to `fallback_fn()` until the cooldown elapses; then one call is tried in `half_open`. A success there returns to `closed`; a failure goes back to `open` for another full cooldown. `fallback_fn` is a required parameter, so the caller has to decide up front what a degraded response looks like. This is single-threaded teaching code: with several threads, more than one caller could pass the cooldown check at the same moment, so a library uses a lock or a permit count for half-open trials. It also treats every exception as the dependency's fault. In production, don't count errors the caller caused (a 400 or a validation failure), or one client sending bad input can open the circuit for everybody. `time.monotonic()` is used because `time.time()` can jump when the system clock is adjusted.

examples.title: Where a Fallback Is Safe vs. Where It Is Not
examples.code:
Dependency: recommendations_service (feature: "customers also bought")
  Fallback when circuit is open: return an empty list / hide the section
  Risk of a wrong fallback: near zero -- a missing suggestion is a minor
  UX downgrade, not a correctness problem

Dependency: payment_authorization_service (feature: "charge the customer")
  Fallback when circuit is open: FAIL the checkout attempt with a clear,
  fast error ("please try again in a moment") -- there is NO safe way to
  fabricate "approved" or "declined" without actually knowing
  Risk of a wrong fallback: severe -- guessing "approved" could ship an
  unpaid order; guessing "declined" could reject a customer who could
  have paid, for no real reason
examples.explanation: The breaker behaves the same way in both cases; the fallback differs because the cost of being wrong differs. 'Just return something reasonable' fails as a blanket policy: an empty list harms nobody in a recommendations widget, while any invented answer to a payment authorization is a business decision made by an error handler. For payments, a fast, clear failure is the fallback. There is a subtle trap in payments as well: a timeout means the result is unknown, since the charge may have gone through before the response was lost. The retry the user makes after 'please try again' must carry the same idempotency key, or it can charge them twice.

misconceptions.description: A circuit breaker is basically the same thing as a timeout -- both are about not waiting too long for a slow dependency.
misconceptions.clarification: A timeout bounds a single call's wait time and operates independently, call by call, with no memory of past calls. A circuit breaker operates on the aggregate pattern across many calls over a window of time, and stops attempting calls for a while once that pattern looks unhealthy. You need both: the breaker only trips after enough failures have been observed, and without a timeout a hanging call never fails, so it is never counted. The first several slow calls before the threshold is reached also need a timeout to bound their own cost, and a breaker doesn't help those. A circuit breaker also has state and memory that a timeout lacks, so it can make a decision for the whole caller (stop attempting calls for a while), where a timeout only ends one attempt.
misconceptions.fact: A timeout bounds a single call's wait time and operates independently, call by call, with no memory of past calls.

misconceptions.description: Tripping a circuit breaker open means the system has failed -- it's a sign something has gone wrong that should be avoided.
misconceptions.clarification: The circuit tripping open is the reliability mechanism working as intended: the failure is whatever made the downstream dependency unhealthy, and it would have happened without a circuit breaker too. Without the breaker, every caller would hang on full timeouts and might cascade into its own outage. Treat a tripped breaker as a signal that something downstream needs attention. A breaker that trips several times a day while the dependency looks healthy is different: its threshold or timeout is probably too tight.
misconceptions.fact: The circuit tripping open is the reliability mechanism working as intended: the failure is whatever made the downstream dependency unhealthy, and it would have happened without a circuit breaker too.

exercises.prompt: A circuit breaker is configured with failure_threshold=5 and cooldown_seconds=20. Starting in the closed state, a downstream dependency begins failing every single call. Trace the breaker's state over the following timeline and predict what a caller experiences at each point: calls 1-5 (each failing), call 6, a call at t=10s into the open period, and a call at t=21s into the open period (assuming the dependency is still down at that point).
exercises.code:
CircuitBreaker(failure_threshold=5, cooldown_seconds=20)
Dependency: every real call fails (simulating an outage)
Calls 1-5: each attempted, each fails
Call 6: attempted shortly after call 5
Call at t=10s after entering open state
Call at t=21s after entering open state (dependency still down)
hints: Track the failure_count across calls 1 through 5 -- at what point does it cross failure_threshold, and what state transition does that trigger?
Once open, does the breaker even attempt the real network call for call 6, or does it go straight to a fallback?
20 seconds is the cooldown. What's different about a call arriving at t=10s (still within cooldown) versus t=21s (just past it)?
exercises.expectedAnswer: Calls 1-5 each attempt the dependency call and each fails (the caller experiences whatever latency/timeout the real call takes, times 5), with failure_count reaching 5 after call 5, tripping the breaker to open. Call 6 is rejected immediately by the breaker: no network call is attempted, and the caller gets the fallback response nearly instantly. The call at t=10s is still within the 20-second cooldown, so it also gets an immediate fallback with no call attempted. The call at t=21s is past the cooldown, so the breaker moves to half-open and allows this one call through as a trial. Since the dependency is still down, the call fails, sending the breaker back to open for another full 20-second cooldown starting from t=21s.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Closed absorbs the first failure_threshold failures at full cost, since each one attempts and waits on the dependency, then trips open. Every call while open is rejected without touching the dependency, however many arrive during the cooldown. Once the cooldown has elapsed, the next call becomes a half-open trial; here it fails, and the breaker returns to open until t=41s. Over the outage, the dependency receives one trial roughly every 20 seconds (plus the time the trial takes to fail) instead of the full request rate. The caller pays too: the request chosen as the trial waits out a full timeout, so one unlucky user per cooldown gets a slow response. Because the trial only happens when a request arrives, a quiet service can stay open well past 20 seconds.

exercises.prompt: A team adds a circuit breaker around calls to a shipping-rate API, but during a real outage of that API, their checkout service still becomes slow and starts timing out for unrelated requests, just as it did before the circuit breaker was added. Here's their integration. Find the bug.
hints: Look at what happens on call 6 and later, after the breaker has recorded enough failures to open. Is the slow API call still attempted every time, with its full timeout?
The circuit breaker pattern is supposed to check the breaker's state BEFORE attempting the call. Does this code check state before calling call_shipping_api at all?
A 15-second timeout per call, times enough concurrent requests, exhausts a thread pool, and a breaker that only observes calls after the fact does nothing to prevent it.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original code always calls `call_shipping_api` first, with its 15-second timeout, and only looks at the breaker's state in the exception handler. Even while the breaker is 'open', every request still waits out a timeout against the dead API, so threads pile up just as they did before: at 20 checkouts per second, 15 seconds each, that is 300 threads stuck at once. The state is recorded correctly and never consulted in time. The fix checks `breaker.state` before the call and only contacts the API when the breaker is closed or half-open. The 15-second timeout is the next thing to change. Until the breaker trips, requests still wait that long, and the five failures it needs can't finish sooner than 15 seconds into the outage, by which time those 300 are already waiting. A timeout near the API's normal worst case, say 1 to 2 seconds, makes the breaker trip much sooner.

assessments.prompt: A service's calls to a downstream dependency are wrapped in a circuit breaker that is currently in the open state. What should happen when a new request needs to call that dependency, and why?
options: The call should be attempted normally, since the circuit breaker only affects logging, not actual call behavior, and refusing to make the call would hide the dependency's true error rate from the team that is responsible for it.
The circuit breaker should immediately close again to give the dependency a chance to prove it has recovered.
The call should be retried up to 10 times with exponential backoff before giving up.

The call should be rejected immediately without attempting the real dependency, using a pre-defined fallback, so the caller doesn't pay the cost (time, threads, connections) of an attempt very likely to fail or hang.
assessments.explanation: Open means: skip the call and return a fallback immediately. That protects the caller's own resources and adds no further load to an already struggling dependency, which is the defining behavior of the open state. The “The call should be attempted normally, since…” option misunderstands the breaker: it gates the calls, and metrics can still record that they were rejected. The “The call should be retried up…” option describes a retry policy, and ten retries against a dependency behind an open circuit is the load the breaker exists to stop. The “The circuit breaker should immediately close again…” option is backwards: the breaker closes only after half-open trial calls succeed, so that an unrecovered dependency isn't flooded again.

assessments.prompt: Explain, to an engineer who has only worked with simple timeouts and retries before, why a circuit breaker is a different and additional tool, and describe a scenario where timeouts and retries alone are not enough to prevent a cascading failure.
assessments.modelAnswer: Timeouts and retries both operate at the level of a single call: a timeout bounds how long one attempt is allowed to hang before giving up, and a retry policy decides whether to try that one call again, usually with some backoff delay, after it fails. Neither remembers anything across calls: each call is treated as if it were the first one ever made to that dependency, and neither reacts to the broader pattern over time. A circuit breaker adds the aggregate view. It watches the success/failure rate across many calls and stops attempting them for a while once the pattern shows the dependency is unhealthy and not having an isolated blip. Imagine a payment-processing dependency that stops responding. Every caller has a 10-second timeout and retries twice with a 1-second backoff between attempts. Without a circuit breaker, every request that needs a payment result attempts up to three calls (initial plus two retries), each waiting up to 10 seconds, for a worst case of 32 seconds per request (3 x 10 + 2 x 1). At 50 requests per second that is 1,600 requests held at once, enough to exhaust the caller's capacity and take down unrelated requests: a cascading failure. A circuit breaker watching the aggregate failure rate would trip open after the first handful of failures, and every request after that gets an immediate, cheap fallback. Timeouts and retries stay in place underneath the breaker to handle transient blips, but alone they can't recognize 'this isn't transient anymore, stop trying.'

assessments.prompt: After a circuit breaker's cooldown period elapses while in the open state, what does the breaker do next?
options: It doubles the cooldown period and waits again before allowing any calls.
It transitions to half-open and allows a small number of trial calls through to test whether the dependency has recovered, closing again on success or reopening for another full cooldown on failure.

It immediately closes and resumes full traffic without any verification that the dependency has recovered, because the cooldown period is always chosen to be longer than the dependency's worst possible outage.
It stays open permanently until an engineer manually resets it.
assessments.explanation: Half-open lets a small number of calls test the dependency: success closes the breaker, and failure reopens it and restarts the cooldown. The “It immediately closes and resumes full traffic…” option skips the verification that half-open exists to provide. The “It stays open permanently until an engineer…” option is wrong: the transition is automatic, though many libraries also offer a manual override. The “It doubles the cooldown period and waits…” option describes an optional refinement: some breakers lengthen the cooldown after a failed trial, but first they make the trial.

assessments.prompt: Why is 'just return something reasonable' a mistake when applied uniformly as the open-state fallback for different dependencies?
options: Because only recommendation services are allowed to have fallbacks; financial services must always attempt the real call regardless of circuit state.
Because circuit breakers should never have a fallback at all -- they should simply raise an unhandled exception.
Because what counts as a safe fallback depends on the cost of being wrong for that feature.
Because fallback functions are always slower to execute than the real dependency call, defeating the purpose of failing fast.
assessments.explanation: An empty recommendations list costs almost nothing. An invented 'approved' ships an unpaid order, and an invented 'declined' turns away a customer who could have paid. The “Because circuit breakers should never have…” option throws away graceful degradation: an unhandled exception fails the page for a dependency it could have done without. The “Because fallback functions are always slower…” option is fabricated: returning a default or cached value takes microseconds. The “Because only recommendation services are allowed…” option is wrong: a payment fallback is allowed, and it is a fast, clear failure.

assessments.prompt: Why is a degraded, hanging dependency more dangerous than one that is cleanly, fully down?
options: A cleanly down dependency is comparatively easy to detect and route around.
There is no meaningful difference -- both failure modes are described as equally dangerous and equally fast to detect.
A degraded dependency always returns incorrect data silently, while a fully down dependency never does.
A cleanly down dependency causes more total network traffic than a degraded one.
assessments.explanation: A dead dependency refuses connections at once, so calls fail in milliseconds and health checks notice. A hanging one keeps each caller waiting until its own timeout fires, holding a thread and a connection the whole time, and may still pass a shallow health check. The “A degraded dependency always returns incorrect data…” option is about data correctness; a slow response is usually a correct one. The “A cleanly down dependency causes more total…” option is fabricated, and traffic volume isn't what exhausts the caller. The “There is no meaningful difference -- both…” option ignores that a hanging call holds resources and a refused one doesn't.

concepts.title: Rate Limiting and Backpressure
concepts.description: A circuit breaker protects a caller from an unhealthy dependency. Rate limiting and backpressure protect a service from its own callers: the same self-protection instinct, aimed at the traffic arriving instead of the traffic going out.
learningObjectives: Explain rate limiting as a self-protection mechanism and distinguish it from capacity planning.
Compare token bucket and fixed/sliding window rate-limiting algorithms and explain the bursty-traffic weakness fixed windows have that token buckets address.
Define backpressure and explain how it differs from rate limiting -- signaling upstream to slow down versus outright rejecting excess requests.
Explain graceful degradation under load (shedding low-priority work first) as a design choice distinct from an uncontrolled, undifferentiated collapse.
Evaluate a system under a traffic spike and recommend an appropriate combination of rate limiting, backpressure, and load shedding.

sections.heading: Rate Limiting: Protecting Yourself From Your Own Callers
sections.body: **Rate limiting** caps how many requests a client, API key, IP address, or tenant may make in a given window, and rejects the excess, typically with HTTP 429. It's easy to see it as a business or fairness tool (stopping one customer from monopolizing shared capacity, enforcing a pricing tier), and it is that. It is also a reliability mechanism. Without a cap, one misbehaving client (a buggy retry loop, a runaway script, a scraper with no backoff) or one legitimate but unexpectedly large burst can use up enough capacity to degrade service for every other caller, or take the service down. This is the bursty-traffic problem from the sync-vs-async lesson attacked from the other side: instead of, or in addition to, building infrastructure that absorbs the burst, you refuse to accept more than an agreed amount from any one source, which turns an unbounded risk into a bounded one.

sections.heading: Token Bucket vs. Fixed Window: Why Bursts at the Boundary Matter
sections.body: A naive **fixed window** limiter ("100 requests per client per 60-second window, resetting on the minute") has a well-known flaw: nothing stops a client from sending 100 requests in the last second of one window and 100 more in the first second of the next, so 200 requests arrive in about two seconds. Each batch is within the stated limit, and the burst is exactly what the limit was meant to prevent. The **token bucket** algorithm avoids this. A bucket holds up to some maximum number of tokens and refills at a steady rate (one token every 600 ms for a 100-per-minute limit); each request takes one token, and a request is rejected if the bucket is empty. That smooths the rate over time instead of only bounding totals inside resettable windows. It still allows a legitimate short burst up to the bucket's capacity (a client that has been idle can spend a full bucket at once) without the boundary-straddling double burst. Capacity sets how big a burst can be, and the refill rate sets the sustained rate. A **sliding window** (a rolling count over the last N seconds instead of a hard reset) fixes the same flaw at the price of more bookkeeping.

sections.heading: Backpressure: Signaling 'Slow Down,' Not Just Rejecting
sections.body:
**Backpressure** is related but distinct. Instead of a hard external cap enforced by rejecting requests, it is a signal that flows backward through a pipeline, from a component that is falling behind to whatever sends it work, so the sender can slow down before things get worse. The classic example is a bounded queue between a producer and a consumer: if the consumer is slower, the queue fills, and once it is full the producer's next enqueue blocks (or fails immediately, depending on the design) until the consumer makes room. The fullness of the queue is the signal. TCP flow control does the same at the network layer: a receiver advertises how much buffer space it has left, and the sender throttles to match instead of sending as fast as it can and letting packets be dropped.

The distinction to keep in a design review: rate limiting is an externally imposed cap at the system's edge (per client, per key), aimed at fairness and abuse prevention as much as self-protection. Backpressure is an internal signal between cooperating components, aimed at keeping a fast producer from overwhelming the slower consumer it feeds. Well-designed systems use both: rate limiting at the API edge bounds what any one external caller can send, and backpressure between internal services and queues keeps any one stage from drowning the next.

sections.heading: Graceful Degradation: Choosing What to Shed, on Purpose
sections.body:
Rate limiting and backpressure both eventually meet the same moment: there is more demand than the system can handle, and something has to give. Without a plan the result is uncontrolled collapse: everything slows together, timeouts cascade, and the system fails severely and at random about who it hurts. **Load shedding** is the deliberate alternative. When overloaded, you reject or degrade some work on purpose so the rest keeps succeeding, following a priority decision made in advance instead of whatever times out first. A search engine under extreme load might serve fast, slightly less relevant results from a cheaper ranking path. A video platform might drop to a lower encoding quality before it drops the stream. An e-commerce API might reject or delay background sync calls while continuing to accept checkouts.

What good examples share is that the most important operations are identified and protected explicitly, and shedding starts from the least important, instead of every request, critical or not, degrading by the same amount as capacity runs out. That requires knowing beforehand which of your endpoints and features matter most, a judgment that is much easier to make in a calm design discussion than in the middle of an incident.

sections.heading: Putting It Together: A Layered Defense
sections.body: In a mature system these mechanisms stack, each catching what the previous one missed. Rate limiting at the edge bounds what any one caller can send, whatever the system's health. Backpressure between internal components keeps a fast stage from overwhelming a slower one it feeds. Circuit breakers (the previous lesson) stop a caller from hammering a dependency that is already unhealthy. Load shedding makes an explicit, prioritized choice about what to sacrifice when demand exceeds total capacity despite all of the above. None of them guarantees a system never has a bad moment under extreme load. What they provide together is that a bad moment stays contained and survivable, and doesn't become an all-or-nothing outage that takes critical and non-critical functionality down for every user at once.

examples.title: Fixed Window's Boundary Burst vs. Token Bucket
examples.code:
Limit: 100 requests per client per 60-second window

FIXED WINDOW (resets exactly on the minute):
  11:00:59.5 - client sends 100 requests -- ALL ALLOWED (window: 11:00:00-11:00:59)
  11:01:00.5 - client sends 100 MORE requests -- ALL ALLOWED (new window: 11:01:00-11:01:59)
  -> 200 requests arrived within about 1 second, both batches technically
     compliant with "100 per 60s" -- the limiter did nothing to stop this

TOKEN BUCKET (capacity 100, refill 1 token per 0.6s = ~100/min steady rate):
  11:00:59.5 - bucket has 100 tokens (client was idle) -- spends all 100, allowed
  11:01:00.5 - only ~1.6 tokens have refilled in that 1 second -- request 2+
               in this second is REJECTED until tokens accumulate again
  -> the boundary-straddling double-burst is prevented, because the token
     bucket has no artificial reset boundary for a client to exploit
examples.explanation: The fixed window's flaw isn't an arithmetic bug: 100 requests in each 60-second window really is within the limit for each window. The limiter has no memory that spans the reset boundary, so a client that knows (or stumbles onto) the reset time can double up right at the seam. The token bucket has no seam: tokens refill continuously, so spending a full bucket and then trying to spend another is impossible until enough time has passed for tokens to regenerate. That is why token bucket or sliding window is the usual recommendation over naive fixed windows wherever boundary bursts matter.

examples.title: A Bounded Queue Providing Backpressure
examples.code:
# Fragment: process() stands for your own work function
import queue

# maxsize=1000 is the key detail -- an UNBOUNDED queue provides NO backpressure at all
work_queue = queue.Queue(maxsize=1000)

def producer(item):
    # blocks here if the queue is full, until the consumer makes room --
    # this block IS the backpressure signal reaching the producer
    work_queue.put(item, block=True, timeout=5)

def consumer():
    while True:
        item = work_queue.get()
        process(item)             # if this is slow, the queue fills up,
        work_queue.task_done()    # and producer.put() calls start blocking
examples.explanation: `maxsize=1000` is what makes this backpressure instead of an unbounded buffer that papers over a capacity mismatch. If `process(item)` is slow relative to arrivals, the queue fills toward 1000 items, and once it is full `work_queue.put(...)` blocks the producer, forcing it down to the consumer's real throughput. An unbounded queue would let the producer keep enqueueing, hiding the mismatch until memory runs out or the wait in an ever-growing queue becomes unacceptable. It delays and obscures overload without preventing it. Note the `timeout=5`: if the queue stays full for 5 seconds, `put` raises `queue.Full`, and the producer has to decide what to do (retry, drop, or return an error to its own caller).

examples.title: Graceful Degradation: Shedding Low-Priority Work First
examples.code:
E-commerce platform under an unexpected 5x traffic spike, capacity exceeded

UNDIFFERENTIATED COLLAPSE (no load shedding):
  Checkout requests, product browsing, and background inventory-sync
  calls all compete equally for the same overloaded resources.
  Latency degrades roughly EQUALLY across all three -- checkout (revenue-
  critical) becomes just as slow and failure-prone as inventory sync
  (non-urgent, can safely run a few minutes late).

GRACEFUL DEGRADATION (explicit priority-based shedding):
  Priority tiers defined in advance: checkout > product browsing >
  background inventory sync.
  Under overload: reject/delay inventory-sync calls FIRST (they can
  safely retry in a few minutes), then throttle product browsing if
  needed (show slightly stale cached data), while continuing to
  accept and fully serve checkout requests without degradation for
  as long as possible.
examples.explanation: Both scenarios face the same 5x spike with the same total capacity. The only difference is whether the system makes a deliberate choice about what to sacrifice. Treating every request as equally important is itself a decision, an accidental one, so the revenue-critical path degrades exactly as much as the least critical one. The graceful version builds a business judgment (checkout must keep working even if other features degrade or pause) into the system's overload behavior, so the parts that matter most survive a spike the platform as a whole can't absorb.

misconceptions.description: Rate limiting and backpressure are the same mechanism with two different names.
misconceptions.clarification: Rate limiting is typically an externally imposed cap at a system's edge, per client or per API key, that rejects requests once a limit is crossed, often for fairness or abuse prevention as much as self-protection. Backpressure is an internal signal flowing backward between cooperating components of one pipeline (a slow consumer signaling a fast producer to slow down, often through a filling queue or a blocked write), meant to keep one internal stage from overwhelming the stage it feeds. They often appear in the same system, solving related but different problems at different layers.
misconceptions.fact: Rate limiting is typically an externally imposed cap at a system's edge, per client or per API key, that rejects requests once a limit is crossed, often for fairness or abuse prevention as much as self-protection.

misconceptions.description: Under heavy load, the fairest thing a system can do is let every request degrade by roughly the same amount, rather than singling any of them out.
misconceptions.clarification: Treating every request identically under overload isn't neutral. It decides implicitly that a revenue-critical checkout and a background analytics sync deserve the same treatment, which is rarely true and rarely what anyone would choose if asked. Graceful degradation through deliberate load shedding makes that decision in advance, so behavior under overload reflects a real priority judgment instead of whatever happens to fail first.

exercises.prompt: A public API enforces a fixed-window rate limit of 1,000 requests per client per hour, resetting exactly on the hour. A client, aware of this reset timing, sends 1,000 requests at 1:59:50pm and another 1,000 requests at 2:00:05pm. Predict whether the rate limiter blocks any of these requests, and how many total requests get through in this roughly 15-second span. Then predict how a token-bucket limiter configured for the same average rate (1,000/hour) would behave for the same traffic pattern.
exercises.code:
Fixed window: 1,000 requests/hour per client, reset on the hour
Client sends: 1,000 requests at 1:59:50pm, then 1,000 more at 2:00:05pm

Token bucket (same average rate): capacity C, refill rate ~0.278 tokens/sec
(1000 tokens per 3600 seconds), configured for equivalent average throughput
hints: Figure out which 60-minute window each batch of 1,000 requests falls into, given the reset happens exactly on the hour.
Under the fixed window, does the limiter have any way to know that 1:59:50pm's batch and 2:00:05pm's batch happened only 15 seconds apart?
For the token bucket, work out how many tokens could plausibly have accumulated by 2:00:05pm if the bucket started empty or partially full after being spent at 1:59:50pm.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The fixed window lets all 2,000 requests through: the first 1,000 fall in the window ending at 2:00:00pm and the second 1,000 in the new window starting then, each within its own limit. The limiter has no memory connecting the windows, so 2,000 requests in about 15 seconds is "compliant". A token bucket with capacity 1,000 (assumed full beforehand) would be emptied by the first batch at 1:59:50pm, and only about 0.278 tokens/sec x 15 s = 4 tokens refill before the second batch arrives. It rejects nearly all of the second batch, lets through only a handful of requests, and then continues at the steady refill rate.
exercises.solutionExplanation: This is the fixed-window boundary burst in its clearest form. The limiter's memory resets at the hour boundary, so two batches 15 seconds apart in real time but on opposite sides of it are evaluated in isolation, letting through double the intended hourly rate in a small fraction of the hour. The token bucket has no reset: its remaining tokens persist across clock boundaries, so a client that emptied its bucket 15 seconds ago can't spend a full bucket again until tokens accumulate at the refill rate, and refilling 1,000 tokens at 0.278 per second takes a full hour. That is why token bucket or sliding window is preferred over fixed windows for stopping boundary-timed bursts, even at the same long-run average rate. Capacity is the knob for burst size: a bucket of 100 would have rejected most of the first batch too.

exercises.prompt: A background job pipeline has a producer generating events much faster than the consumer can process them. The team used an unbounded in-memory queue between them, reasoning 'the queue will handle any speed mismatch.' After a few hours of sustained high producer throughput, the consumer process is OOM-killed and events queued in memory are lost entirely. Diagnose why the queue didn't actually solve the mismatch and propose a fix.
hints: If the consumer is reliably slower than the producer, what happens to the NUMBER OF ITEMS sitting in an unbounded queue over time -- does it stay roughly constant, or does it grow without limit?
An unbounded queue lets the producer keep calling put() successfully no matter how large the queue already is -- does the producer ever get a signal that it's outpacing the consumer?
Where is all of this growing, unprocessed queue data actually being stored, and what's the consequence of that data structure growing indefinitely on a machine with finite memory?
exercises.solutionExplanation: An unbounded queue doesn't solve a producer/consumer speed mismatch. It hides it: the queue grows without limit for as long as the producer outpaces the consumer, which here is hours. Every queued event lives in process memory, so an ever-growing queue is an ever-growing allocation with no ceiling, and eventually the OS kills the process (OOM), losing every event still in the queue, because an in-memory queue has no durability. The fix is to bound the queue and let a full queue block (or otherwise signal) the producer. That is backpressure: instead of memory growing silently until an unplanned failure, the producer is forced down to the consumer's sustained throughput as soon as the queue fills, which trades a hidden, unbounded risk for a visible, bounded slowdown. If losing events is unacceptable even temporarily, a durable, disk-backed message queue (covered earlier in this subject) is stronger than a bounded in-memory queue, because it survives a restart.

assessments.prompt: A team notices that their fixed-window rate limiter (1,000 requests/hour, reset on the hour) allows some clients to send nearly 2,000 requests within a few seconds by timing requests around the window boundary. Which alternative most directly fixes this specific weakness while preserving roughly the same long-run average allowed rate?
options: Lower the limit to 500 requests per hour.
Increase the window from 1 hour to 24 hours.
Add a circuit breaker in front of the rate limiter.
Switch to a token bucket (or sliding window) approach, where allowance accumulates continuously over time rather than resetting completely at a fixed clock boundary.
assessments.explanation: The weakness comes from the limiter's memory resetting fully at a fixed clock boundary, so two windows' worth of allowance can be spent back to back around it. Token bucket and sliding window remove the reset: allowance is tracked continuously, so there is no seam to exploit. The “Lower the limit to 500 requests per hour” option changes the total allowed and leaves the boundary exploit in place: a client could still send about 500 near one boundary and 500 near the next. The “Add a circuit breaker in front…” option addresses a different problem (protecting a caller from an unhealthy dependency), not inbound limiting. The “Increase the window from 1 hour to 24 hours” option only moves the boundary: the same straddling trick works once a day instead of once an hour, and the possible burst gets larger relative to the intended steady rate.

assessments.prompt: A colleague asks: "If we already have circuit breakers protecting our service from unhealthy dependencies, why do we also need rate limiting and backpressure?" Explain what gap circuit breakers leave open that these two mechanisms close.
assessments.modelAnswer: Both are self-protection, but they guard against traffic flowing in opposite directions, and neither substitutes for the other. A circuit breaker sits on the outbound side. It protects a service from a downstream dependency that it calls and that has become unhealthy, by no longer sending calls that will probably fail or hang and by failing fast so the service's own resources aren't consumed waiting on them. It says nothing about traffic arriving at the service from its own callers. If a client, or a burst of legitimate traffic, sends far more requests than the service can handle, the breaker offers no protection, because no unhealthy dependency is involved: the service itself is what's overwhelmed. Rate limiting and backpressure close that gap. Rate limiting caps how much any single external caller may send, protecting the service from abuse, bugs, or unexpected volume. Backpressure does the same job internally: a slower component signals the faster one feeding it to slow down, so an overloaded stage isn't buried by the one in front of it. A complete reliability story covers both directions: breakers so the service isn't dragged down by what it depends on, and rate limiting and backpressure so it isn't overwhelmed by what depends on it, or by its own pipeline getting out of balance. A service with excellent breakers and no rate limiting can still be taken down by a traffic spike or an abusive client.

assessments.prompt: A bounded queue sits between a fast producer and a slower consumer. Once the queue fills to its maximum size, the producer's next enqueue call blocks until the consumer makes room. What concept does this illustrate, and how does it differ from rate limiting?
options: This is load shedding, since the producer's work is being discarded once the queue is full.

This is backpressure -- an internal signal flowing backward from a slower component to a faster one feeding it, forcing the producer to slow down to match the consumer's real throughput, distinct from rate limiting's externally imposed, per-client cap enforced at a system's edge.
This is rate limiting, since both mechanisms reject excess work once a cap is reached.
This is a circuit breaker, since the queue is 'tripping open' once full.
assessments.explanation: This is backpressure: when the bounded queue fills, the producer's next enqueue blocks until the consumer makes room, so the queue's fullness is the signal. Rate limiting differs: it is an externally imposed cap at the system's edge, usually per client, and it rejects requests. The “This is rate limiting, since both mechanisms…” option conflates the two. The “This is a circuit breaker, since…” option applies breaker terminology to something that tracks no dependency health. The “This is load shedding, since the producer's…” option is wrong: the producer blocks, and nothing is discarded.

assessments.prompt: What distinguishes graceful degradation from an uncontrolled, undifferentiated collapse under overload?
options: Graceful degradation deliberately identifies and protects the most important operations in advance, shedding load starting from the least important, rather than letting every request -- critical or not -- degrade by the same uniform amount.
Graceful degradation happens automatically in every system without any advance design work.
Graceful degradation means the system never rejects any requests, no matter how overloaded it becomes.
Graceful degradation is only possible if the system uses a token-bucket rate limiter instead of a fixed window.
assessments.explanation: Graceful degradation identifies and protects the most important operations in advance and sheds load starting from the least important, where an uncontrolled collapse lets every request, critical or not, degrade by the same amount. The “Graceful degradation happens automatically in every system…” option is wrong because it takes deliberate design work. The “Graceful degradation means the system never rejects…” option is false: it involves rejecting or delaying lower-priority requests. The “Graceful degradation is only possible…” option invents a dependency on one rate-limiting algorithm.

assessments.prompt: Why is rate limiting more than just a business or fairness mechanism?
options: Because rate limiting always increases a service's total throughput capacity.
Because rate limiting is required by law in most jurisdictions for any public API.

Because without some cap, a single misbehaving client or an unexpectedly large legitimate burst can consume enough capacity to degrade or take down service for every other caller, making rate limiting a reliability mechanism in its own right.
Because fairness and business concerns are not real reasons to implement rate limiting at all.
assessments.explanation: Without some cap, a single misbehaving client or an unexpectedly large legitimate burst can consume enough capacity to degrade or take down service for every other caller, so rate limiting is a reliability mechanism as well. The “Because rate limiting is required by law…” option invents a legal requirement. The “Because fairness and business concerns…” option is wrong: those are real reasons, just not the only ones. The “Because rate limiting always increases a service's…” option is false: it caps and rejects traffic and doesn't add capacity.

assessments.prompt: A partner's buggy integration sent 50 times its normal traffic to your public API, which slowed down every other customer. Design the protections you would add.
assessments.modelAnswer: Isolate tenants so one client cannot consume everyone's capacity. Add rate limiting per API key at the edge or API gateway, using a token bucket or sliding window algorithm backed by a shared store such as Redis so limits hold across instances, and return 429 with a Retry-After header so well-behaved clients back off. Set different quotas per plan and a global limit to protect the service overall. Inside the system apply backpressure: bounded queues and connection pools, timeouts on downstream calls, and load shedding that rejects low-priority work when latency rises instead of letting everything slow down. Circuit breakers stop cascading failures to dependencies. Monitor per-client request rates and alert on anomalies, and document limits so partners can design retries with exponential backoff and jitter.
